title: Specialist cleaning method boundaries
audience: Supervisors and cleaners deciding which cleaning methods are within a cleaner's boundary for exhaust systems.
learningOutcomes: Identify which cleaning methods sit within routine boundaries and which are specialist methods.
Explain why a specialist method is not used by a general cleaner.
Refuse to offer or agree to a specialist method without eligibility and written scope.

instruction.heading: Method is a boundary, not a preference
instruction.body: When people talk about cleaning an exhaust system, they often name a method: wipe, soak, scrape, brush, spray, foam, steam, pressure-wash or 'degrease'. Each method carries a different risk. A wipe on an accessible hood surface is a different task from a brush run through a duct, and a foam applied in an enclosed canopy void is different again. The method you choose decides what you touch, what you disturb, what you wet, what you spread, and what chemical you expose yourself and others to. For that reason, the method is a boundary, and you must check it before you choose a tool. This lesson separates the methods that sit within a routine boundary from those that are specialist methods. It also explains how to refuse a specialist method politely and in writing, without offering it as a favour.

instruction.heading: Routine boundary and specialist methods
instruction.body: A routine method is one that the written scope and the site procedure both allow for an accessible surface, with a product named in the site's approved list and a safety data sheet on file. In practice, that can include wiping an accessible hood surface with an approved detergent, and cleaning removable filters in the place the site designates. Those examples are teaching examples. The site decides what is routine, and it must be written down. A specialist method is one that reaches into concealed or connected parts of the system, changes the system's condition, requires isolation, opening of access panels, use of equipment that is not approved for the site, or chemistry outside the approved list. Internal duct cleaning by brush, air or mechanical means is specialist. So are fan internals, fire-suppression components, and any roof or high-access work. Chemical methods for concealed or heavily fouled surfaces are specialist unless the site has approved them and the person applying them is eligible. When a method is not clearly routine, treat it as specialist until the site says otherwise.

instruction.heading: Detergent, degreaser and sanitiser are different tasks
instruction.body: Chemistry is part of the method. Detergents remove dirt and grease from a surface but do not, on their own, kill micro-organisms. Sanitisers destroy micro-organisms, but some sanitisers must be rinsed off and others are food-safe only when used as directed. Degreasers are formulated to dissolve heavy oily residue and are often more aggressive. Western Australia's health guidance for food premises describes this difference between detergents and sanitisers, and gives example heat-and-chemical steps for food-contact utensils and surfaces; those steps are a food-premises practice, not an exhaust-cleaning method, and the Food Standards Code clauses that the guidance cites were not read for this lesson. For exhaust work, the question is simpler: which product is approved for this surface, what does its safety data sheet say about handling, dilution, ventilation and disposal, and is the product within the scope you were given? If the answer to any of those is unclear, the method is not routine.

instruction.heading: Why a general cleaner does not take on specialist methods
instruction.body: A general cleaner may be competent at routine surface work and still be outside the eligibility, equipment and authority needed for a specialist method. Specialist methods can spread contamination into areas that were not cleaned, disturb grease that was previously stable, damage components that protect against fire, or create a hazard for the next person who opens the system. The specialist also needs to see the condition of the system before work starts, and that often means access the cleaner does not have. This is why the question is not 'can I do it?' but 'am I eligible and authorised to do it, in writing, for this part of the system?' When the answer is no, the method is declined and referred. Declining is not a failure of service. It protects the customer, the site and the cleaner, and it keeps the record accurate.

instruction.heading: Refusing and referring a specialist method
instruction.body: When a client or supervisor asks for a specialist method, state the method you have been asked to use, say which boundary it crosses, and say what you are able to do within your scope. Do not offer a 'quick version' of the specialist method, and do not agree to try it. Give the request to the person who can approve a change of scope, and record it. If the request comes from a sales conversation, the cleaner should not quote a specialist price or promise a result. Keep the message short and factual. A written method change, if approved, should name the method, the layer, the products, the people who will do the work, the eligibility held, the access arrangements and the exclusions. Until that document exists, the specialist method is not authorised.

procedure: Read the written scope and the site procedure before choosing any method.
Name the method you have been asked to use, and the part of the system it reaches.
Decide whether the method is routine, meaning it is allowed for an accessible surface and the product is on the approved list. If it is not clearly routine, treat it as specialist.
Check the safety data sheet for any product the method uses, and confirm the dilution, ventilation and disposal points before opening the container.
For a specialist method, decline the work, record the request, and refer it to the person who can approve a change of scope.
Do not offer a partial or quick version of a specialist method, and do not quote a price or result for it.
Where a specialist method is later approved in writing, confirm the eligibility of each person who will do the work before work starts.

workedExamples.situation: The owner of a café asks you to brush the inside of the extraction duct from the hood access point, because the duct 'is greasy and should go with the hood clean'.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which method boundary applies, and what do you say?
workedExamples.reasoning: Brushing an internal duct is a specialist method that reaches a concealed part of the system. It is outside the routine boundary and outside the scope you were given. Decline it and do not open the access point. Tell the owner that the internal duct is a specialist layer and that the request has been recorded and passed to the person who can approve a change of scope. Do not offer to 'just do the first section'.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor asks you to clean the removable filters in the wash area. The site procedure names an approved detergent for filters and designates a sink for the purpose.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is this a routine method, and what checks do you make before you start?
workedExamples.reasoning: Filter cleaning in the designated place with the approved detergent can be a routine method, if the written scope includes filters and the site procedure allows the method. Check the detergent's safety data sheet for dilution, ventilation and disposal, and wear the PPE the sheet and the risk assessment require. Record the method, the product and the place used. If the procedure does not name the sink or the product, treat the method as not yet routine and ask.

workedExamples.situation: A contractor asks you to use a high-strength degreaser foam inside an enclosed canopy void that the site has not previously opened, because the foam is 'quicker than scraping'.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct response, and which checks apply?
workedExamples.reasoning: The method reaches a concealed area, uses a chemical outside the approved list, and may involve ventilation and handling questions that the scope does not address. Decline it. Ask for the product's safety data sheet and for the site's written decision, and refer the request. Do not start the foam application, and do not inspect the void to decide the method yourself.

equipmentAndPpe: Written scope and site procedure stating the approved methods and products.
Safety data sheets for each approved product, kept with the job file.
Method change request form, for any request outside the routine boundary.
PPE as set by the product's safety data sheet and the task risk assessment, such as chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection where the sheet requires them.
Labelled containers for approved products, with dilution noted where the label or sheet requires it.

commonErrors.error: Treating every hood-related task as routine because the hood is in scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each method against the written scope and the approved product list before choosing a tool.

commonErrors.error: Offering a quick version of a specialist method to keep the client happy.
commonErrors.prevention: Decline the method, record the request, and refer it. Do not offer partial specialist work.

commonErrors.error: Using a degreaser or sanitiser because it is on the shelf, without checking its safety data sheet.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the safety data sheet for handling, dilution, ventilation and disposal, and check the product is on the approved list.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a specialist price or result during a sales conversation.
commonErrors.prevention: Pass the enquiry to the authorised person. Quote only for work that the written scope and your eligibility cover.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A safety data sheet must be prepared by the manufacturer or importer of a hazardous chemical, must be reviewed at least every five years, and must cover handling, storage, disposal, and health and emergency measures. The site procedure requires a copy of the safety data sheet to be kept on site.
This lesson does not grant approval for specialist cleaning methods on exhaust systems; the site procedure governs.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority. Specialist methods must be performed only by people who hold the eligibility the task requires, under a written scope.

qualityStandard: Each method in the desk exercise is labelled routine or specialist, with the reason stated.
The internal duct request in the worked example is declined without any work started or access point opened.
No specialist method is offered, partially performed or quoted without written scope and eligibility.
documentationEvidence: Method classification record for each method considered, with the reason.
Safety data sheet reference for each product used, with the date it was checked.
Method change request and the written decision, or the record that the request was declined and referred.
summary: Method is a boundary: check it against the written scope before choosing a tool.
Specialist methods reach concealed or connected parts of the system or use chemistry outside the approved list.
Decline and refer specialist methods in writing. Do not offer partial work or quote for it.
Check each product's safety data sheet before use, and record the product and its reference.

knowledgeChecks.question: Is brushing the internal duct from an access point a routine method for a general cleaner?
options: Yes, because it is part of the same system as the hood and is cleaned with it
No, it reaches a concealed part of the system and is a specialist method
Yes, if the client agrees to it in conversation with the cleaner first

knowledgeChecks.question: What defines the cleaner's method boundary?
options: The method the cleaner is most experienced with on other sites
The written scope, the site procedure and the approved product list
Whatever tool is available on the day of the clean at the site

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks you to add a specialist method to the job. What is correct?
options: Agree and try a quick version to see how it goes for the owner and the crew on the day with the team
Record the request, decline the specialist method, and refer it to the person who can approve a change of scope
Quote a price and start the work once the client pays the deposit that was asked for on the day
